title: 3-Read Friday #59: AI in the Classroom, Coaching, and Written Comments
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 59 leans heavily into AI's practical classroom use, bookending a coaching piece between two AI-focused recommendations. Barton opens with a Durrington Research School post describing how a head of maths used ChatGPT to speed up vocabulary-instruction resource creation, explicitly framing his interest as being in 'concrete examples of how teachers use AI to do their jobs quicker or better' rather than AI hype in the abstract. He then recommends Sarah Cottingham's short 'coaching cut' on using 'what if' questions to deepen a coachee's thinking, calling her blog 'a source of gold' for anyone doing coaching or lesson observations. His third pick is Daisy Christodoulou's follow-up post proposing comparative-judgement-plus-AI as a 'best of both worlds' alternative to individualised written comments, which he says 'has real potential'.
points: Barton's explicit statement of interest -- concrete AI time-savings over abstract AI hype -- functions as an implicit editorial standard he applies across all his AI-related picks in this era of the newsletter.
His repeated praise of Cottingham's Cognitive Coaching Substack ('a source of gold') across multiple issues in this batch shows a sustained, not one-off, endorsement of her coaching content.

He flags Christodoulou's comparative-judgement-plus-AI proposal as having 'real potential' -- a stronger and more forward-looking endorsement than his usual descriptive summaries, suggesting he sees it as a genuine solution rather than just an interesting idea.

Grouping a teacher-AI-workflow story, a coaching technique, and an AI-feedback proposal in one issue shows Barton treating 'AI in schools' as a theme spanning multiple distinct use cases (resource creation, feedback) rather than a single monolithic topic.
quotes: The world may be AI-obsessed, but I am interested in concrete examples of how teachers use AI to do their jobs quicker or better.
